samples.hyp: To assess the necessary metrics for mass testing of SARS-CoV-2 for the potential control of the outbreak in the large province of Lusaka in Zambia, a focus was placed on individuals who are asymptomatic:
Research on the use of a simple mathematical model

The novel Coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa is observed with a high number of asymptomatic individuals (or those showing mild symptoms) suspected to play a role in the spread of the infection.
The actual statistics and magnitude of transmissions among asymptomatic individuals are not clearly evident.
However, studies highlight the importance of developing strategies to control the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a simplified and accurate mathematical model of the susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) type to assess the impact of implementing measures to isolate individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2 but asymptomatic, through mass testing, to control the spread of the disease in the Lusaka Province of Zambia.
Here we presented two scenarios; (1) assuming that asymptomatic individuals account for 70% of all COVID-19 cases and (2) that asymptomatic individuals account for only 50% of the cases.

Conversely, the model was evaluated under the initial assumption that asymptomatic individuals could spread the disease similarly to symptomatic individuals, and secondly, a similar assumption that asymptomatic individuals could spread the disease only half as much as those with symptoms.

In a model assuming that 70% of cases are asymptomatic, a minimum testing rate of ≥ 7911 tests per 100,000 people would be sufficient to control the spread of the disease if asymptomatic individuals are only half as infectious as those who are symptomatic, whereas if it is assumed that the transmission is equal, then a rate of ≥ 10028 tests per 100,000 people would be required.

In 50% of those who were asymptomatic, lower thresholds of mass testing ≥ 4540 tests/100000 population were sufficient to control the secondary spread of estimated transmission rates among asymptomatic individuals compared to those who were symptomatic.
Interactions and outcomes

Our model suggests that implementing measures to isolate COVID-19 cases, including asymptomatic individuals, with comprehensive testing could be used as an appropriate control measure for the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, but it will require a significant amount of funding.
Conducting mass testing in major cities such as Lusaka could reduce the spread of COVID-19, but is that feasible?

In 2020, computer models suggested that the spread of COVID-19 in metropolitan areas could be better controlled by conducting mass testing of people, and by isolating all those whose tests indicated they were infected.
However, researchers have stated that this method could be costly and may not be feasible.
After the outbreak of the pandemic, most people who were infected with COVID-19 did not show symptoms of the disease and continued to spread the illness to others.
Some studies have suggested that 50% to 80% of people who were infected with COVID-19 were asymptomatic (did not show symptoms) and may have been responsible for 40% to 70% of new transmissions.
Researchers wanted to know if identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals could help control the spread of COVID-19.
They also wanted to know if mass testing, which involves conducting tests on a large number of people without discrimination, helps in identifying asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers have developed a computer model that predicts how people transition from a state of suspicion to one of confrontation, infection, and exclusion.
They focused on data from the Lusaka province in Zambia, which is a commercial hub with an international airport that shares borders with two countries.

Due to the fact that COVID-19 symptoms vary by location, they considered 4 scenarios, where there could be 50% or 70% of COVID-19 cases in people who do not show symptoms, and those cases could be fully or partially transmissible like those that show symptoms.

The researchers' report revealed that it was possible to control the spread of COVID-19 by conducting mass testing and isolating individuals who were found to be infected, including those without symptoms.
They stated that to ensure a noticeable reduction of 90% in the incidence of diseases across all scenarios, it was necessary for 10% of the residents of Lusaka to be tested daily.
They also found that if we wanted the number of new COVID-19 infections to remain unchanged, 22% of people needed to be tested daily.
Even though Zambia had put in place many measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19, cases continued to rise.
Conducting mass human trials reduced the number of COVID-19 cases by 90% in a small town in Italy.
However, there are no previous studies indicating that this will work effectively in a large city elsewhere.

Note that researchers did not conduct mass human trials in these studies; however, they developed a model suggesting that mass human trials could be a solution to reduce the spread of COVID-19 in metropolitan areas.
However, they noted that the possibility of doing so might require a significant amount of money.
They also stated that it is highly possible when combined with other measures, such as travel restrictions, tracking patients, and obtaining a vaccine.
Researchers from Zambia emphasized that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases were very prevalent in Africa at that time.
A summary of the variation in clinical data across African populations due to genetic and environmental differences.
African populations are given genetic assessments in genetic-related studies but they have significant genetic differences and face very different environmental conditions worldwide.

Since evaluations of genetic prediction systems have not yet been conducted on ancient human remains regarding African diversity, we combined polygenic risk score (PRS) data with surveys across Africa and research information from South Africa, Uganda, and the UK to better understand the inclusivity of genetic-related research.
The accuracy of PRS improves with discovery cohorts that include long-deceased individuals compared to studies that do not include long-deceased individuals.

Within the diverse South Africa regarding people who have long passed away and their ethnicities, we discovered that the accuracy of PRS varies across all variables but differs across different groups of people.

The genetic diversity of long-deceased individuals in Africa has a greater impact on the accuracy of PRS compared to other group differences observed among people in the UK when compared to those in Uganda.

We used computers regarding PRS on ancient African individuals using studies on current European genes only when compared to those of ancient individuals; this increased difference resulted in a significantly higher accuracy found in the concentration of hemoglobin and the number of white blood cells, and this indicates significant differences filled with the genes of ancient individuals regarding the genes known to influence sickle cell anemia and allele variation.
Differences in the accuracy of PRS across African populations from different regions are significant compared to those of non-African populations, and this requires a foundational approach.
Why can't we predict genetic diseases in people of African descent?
Researchers state that the current methods used to predict whether a person may have a genetic disease or not do not work effectively for people of African descent.
This is because the data storage related to these analyses often describes the genes of people of European descent.
The GWAS Information Repository stands for "Genome-Wide Association Studies," and scientists use it to investigate patterns and diseases according to genetics.
Indeed, they can use GWAS to associate human genetic risk with disease or with mutations.
Most of the genetic information from GWAS, however, comes from people of European descent.
In these studies, researchers wanted to understand how well this approach can predict the risk of disease in genes using GWAS and how effectively it works in people of African descent.
They also wanted to see if a highly diverse GWAS, in other words, a data repository that includes genetic information, could improve predictions.
This combination is scientifically known as "polygenic risk scores", or PRS.

They used computers to integrate the suggested genetic risks of the African population using GWAS, and they used medical reports of African individuals to examine specific mutations or diseases that could have been caused by genetic mutations.
When using the European GWAS, they discovered that the genetic risk scores were more accurate when individuals were of European descent compared to those of African descent for many variations.

They stated that the risk factors are generally low among African populations because there is a significant difference within this community, which does not align with what we observe in European ancestry.
They also stated that the accuracy of PRS increases as the African ancestry decreases.
The populations in Ethiopia have better perceptions of genetic diseases as they are very similar genetically to European populations.
When we use a highly diverse GWAS that includes people of African descent, the accuracy of predictions improves.
The prediction of blood diseases was highly accurate.
Previous studies have shown that PRS is low in African populations, indicating that the GWAS data repository underestimates the genetic disease risk for individuals of African descent.
However, we know that this is not true.

Research explains that these genetic disease findings are due to African genes being underrepresented in GWAS databases, thus the current value of PRS does not help in predicting genetic diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that it would be better to use a highly diverse information repository that includes genetic information of people of African descent.
Further work is needed to diversify GWAS to include African ancestry so that we can more accurately predict genetic diseases in African populations.
The authors of these studies were from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
Evaluation of Screening and Research Interventions in Preventing Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
Women numbering 851,340 in Namibia are at risk of contracting human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, which can cause cervical cancer.
The evaluation of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy has been proven to be highly effective.
However, data related to the impact of cervical cancer screening programs is lacking.
The research examined the evaluation of surveillance and intervention in the prevention of cervical intraepithelial lesions (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.
Findings showed that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at a higher risk of testing positive for VIA infection.
Older women, especially those with HIV, are more likely to be diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) when treated.

The VIA procedure appears to be beneficial for screening, although the examination of the cervix with acetic acid to assess the condition of patients in the Namibian region should be re-evaluated and used in conjunction with the results of HR-HPV testing.
It is recommended that there be screening methods that include conducting HPV tests on people of different ages and those at risk (for example, those with HIV infection, autoimmune diseases).

Increasing the number of tests can be improved through efforts that utilize previous treatment outcomes, women's health goals, knowledge that aligns with reasons and practices related to national events.
Women in Namibia who are at risk of cervical cancer should be tested and receive treatment early.
Many tests can indicate the risk of cervical cancer in women, but regular tests in Namibia do not consistently use these tests.
Researchers suggest that regular tests be conducted to obtain early warning signs, which could prevent women from being affected by this severe disease.
Cervical cancer (cancer of the lower part of the uterus) causes many deaths among women worldwide.
One of the common causes of cervical cancer is the Human Papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that damages cervical cells, forming lesions called warts, which can eventually cause very severe cancer.
Although there is a vaccine to prevent HPV, the majority of women in African countries, including Namibia, are unable to access it.
This indicates that conducting virus tests or screenings that it causes is crucial for women, as it is the best way to help prevent cancer.
Researchers in these studies state that hospitals lack proper guidelines and information regarding the best practices that can be used.
They add that healthcare workers also lack complete information about how factors such as age or health affect a woman's risk of contracting HPV and cancer.
They conducted research on how some common types of tests (known as screening methods) have effectively worked in detecting HPV and lesions.
They were also interested in comparing testing methods, for example, obtaining cells from the cervix to assess damage compared to just searching for lesions.
They also wanted to know if there were differences among women, such as their age, or if they had other diseases like HIV, which affected their chances of contracting HPV and cancer.
Knowing this information can help hospitals and clinics to use diagnostic methods appropriately.
Researchers examined the medical records of 214 women who had been tested and treated for HPV, cervical lesions, and cervical cancer at a hospital in Windhoek, Namibia.
They focused greatly on early-detected cervical cancer, which can be treated much more easily and effectively.
They collected information on each woman's age and her overall health status.

By examining these records, they found that different testing methods often provide healthcare workers with varying information, and that it can be very beneficial either before or after HPV progresses to cancer.
For example, cancer was often detected through the discovery and examination of cervical cells.
However, lesions can often be detected through visual inspection using a method called "visual inspection with acetic acid" (VIA).
The advantage of this method is that it helps doctors to quickly identify diseases and does not require a lot of money.
It is because it uses basic medical instruments used in women's examinations during pregnancy, such as a speculum (a metal instrument used to look inside the vagina).
They also found that combining different methods often helps doctors with more information about a woman's risk of developing cancer, especially in various tests.
Moreover, researchers found that older women, especially those with HIV, were at a higher risk of being diagnosed with cancer when treated, therefore frequent screening could be very important.
Researchers added that it is a very small number of women who have been tested for HPV (before seeking treatment) even though tests are available.
Doing so could be an important way to detect the disease early.

In general, they stated that their results indicated that it was necessary for the healthcare program in Namibia to carefully plan the implementation of HPV and cervical cancer prevention strategies, using cost-effective methods that effectively detect diseases as early as possible.
The research was a collaboration between scientists from Namibia and South Africa.
Treatment opportunities for co-infection of HBV/HIV compared to single HBV infection in the treatment sector in South Africa

Motivated by international goals to eliminate the hepatitis B virus (HBV), we began to identify individuals with a single HBV infection among those with dual HBV/HIV infections, with the aim of analyzing the impact of treatment and assessing improvements in therapeutic care.
We report on the information we obtained from this diverse cohort of 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), at a university hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
HIV prevalence was present in 39 (34%) of the study participants.
We published cross-sectional data on human subjects, including clinical and laboratory information.

Compared to those with HIV co-infection, adults with HBV monoinfection were less likely to be HBeAg positive (p=0.01), less likely to have been assessed by elastography (p<0.0001), and less likely to be on antiviral therapy (p<0.0001); they were more likely to have detectable HBV viraemia (p=0.04), and more likely to have signs of liver disease including moderate/severe thrombocytopenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and elevated APRI scores (p=0.02).
All three cases of liver cell cancer were associated with a single HBV infection.

Our information indicates that individuals with a single HBV infection may lack opportunities compared to those with a co-infection of HIV, and this suggests the possibility of inequality in referring patients for treatment, care, and management.
Researchers provide recommendations to improve the treatment of hepatitis B.

In recent studies, researchers were able to demonstrate how being co-infected with both hepatitis B (HBV) and the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may increase the likelihood of receiving treatment compared to being infected with HBV alone.
In Southern Africa, chronic infection due to HBV and HIV transmission is a major problem.
Doctors need to understand how these viruses and drugs are used to treat related diseases, so that they can better treat and care for patients.
Researchers wanted to compare the treatment outcomes of patients who had only HBV, with those of patients who had both HBV and HIV.
In this study, researchers enrolled 115 adult patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
They were registered from Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Some patients were infected with HIV (39) and all others were infected with HBV.
Researchers examined species, age, and gender and conducted various clinical and laboratory tests.

They discovered that patients who were only infected with HBV had a low likelihood of taking antiviral drugs, showing natural signs of liver disease (as HBV is a virus that can cause chronic liver disease).

Researchers were able to demonstrate that individuals infected with only HBV had a different likelihood compared to those infected with both HIV and HBV, as patients infected with both viruses were likely to be taking antiretroviral drugs for HIV, which also provides benefits in combating HBV infection.

Results from the studies indicated the potential impact of disparities between referring patients for treatment, caring for them, and treatment options for HBV when compared to co-infection of HIV and HBV, thus providing those infected with both HIV and HBV an opportunity.
Researchers have indicated that we need to improve and provide safe and appropriate services to patients who are infected with HBV only.
One limitation of these studies is the small population size that was only studied in one country and their methods of referring them to the hospital.
In some cases, more advanced hospital settings may show better outcomes compared to what was found in the studies.
Further research will need to be conducted with the aim of truly understanding the differences found in the studies.
This research paper demonstrated the strength of collaboration, where researchers working on this project come from South Africa and the United Kingdom.
By using patients from South Africa in the studies, it is relevant to the part of the African population.
Furthermore, research can help develop better treatment strategies for those with HBV, HIV, or both.
Analysis of the Impact of Insecurity on Women's Entrepreneurial Activities in the SHIRORO Local Government Area of Niger State

The research examined the impact of insecurity on women's entrepreneurial activities in the Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, focusing particularly on women's financial independence initiatives, the types of entrepreneurial activities common among them, and the role of insecurity in their entrepreneurial efforts.

A sample of 377 women was examined, and it resulted in findings that women in Shiroro are highly entrepreneurial where there is a high level of financial dependency, with a strong focus on small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

Research has also found that although the lack of security significantly impacts women's entrepreneurial activities through loss or collapse of assets among other things, the number of women starting businesses has not experienced a significant decrease.

Research suggests that sustainable programs to improve women's access to financial services and usage should be established, and community-based organizations should also be established and strengthened to combat the lack of security in the research sector.
Women entrepreneurs in Niger need more protection.
Researchers have discovered that female entrepreneurs in Niger are highly entrepreneurial and financially independent, but security against losses is a problem.
Researchers wanted to know how safe and secure women running businesses in the Shiroro Local Government Area are, and how this could affect their businesses and financial independence.
They asked 377 women questions about the challenges they face in their area regarding their entrepreneurial activities, financial independence, and lack of security.
They reported that 43% of women said they did not trust men to give them money, and 32% said they had other people they trusted with money.
Researchers also found that 85% of women were earning money in various businesses, and only a few reported that they relied on salaries.
Approximately 56% made money through farming, while 79% through selling.
About 1 in 5 women earned money by braiding hair, sewing, weaving, or washing clothes.
The majority of women (91%) told researchers that their businesses were affected by their fear of being attacked by thieves and vandals.
They lost money and their husbands due to these attacks, sometimes forcing them to raise their children alone.
Women also reported that they do not have sufficient skills and funds to expand their businesses.
Researchers reported that despite these challenges, women in Niger have continued to perform very well in their businesses.
They stated that Shiroro had people of different ethnicities and religions, and this was also suitable for business.
Research challenges the findings of other researchers who reported that women are less successful in their businesses because they are caregivers at home.
In that area, researchers state that the success of women entrepreneurs in the Niger region is greatly affected by the threat of attacks by bandits and thieves.
Researchers suggested that all stakeholders should come together to combat factors that could hinder success in business.
For example, women in Niger should have increased access to financial, agricultural, and security assistance.
They also suggested that women could form groups that could help them combat thieves and vandals.
The Deficiency of Selenium, Copper, and Zinc in Pregnant Women is Associated with the Risk of Preterm Birth: An Observational Study from Malawi
Preterm birth is giving birth before a pregnant woman completes 37 weeks of pregnancy.
Research was conducted to analyze the relationship between the serum of a pregnant woman and selenium, copper, and zinc, and preterm birth.
There were 181 women in the study who were categorized into groups, 90/181 (49.7%) who delivered on time and 91/181 (50.3%) who delivered prematurely.

The mean concentration of serum selenium was 77.0; SD 19.4µg/L, copper was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and zinc was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L compared to the reference values of 47-142µg/L, 0.76-1.59mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, respectively.
The results showed that there was no deficiency of selenium or zinc; and a high concentration of copper serum during pregnancy.
Preterm birth has been associated with genetic variants of copper and zinc metabolism in pregnant women.
Zinc, copper, and selenium compounds associated with preterm birth
Researchers found high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who had preterm births, but in this case, they do not know if these high levels come from the food they consume.
Preterm birth occurs when a woman gives birth to a baby before completing 37 weeks of pregnancy.
Preterm birth is associated with adverse health outcomes for the infant, ranging from birth complications to death.
There can be many factors causing preterm birth, but the role played by a high mixture of micronutrients found in food and the environment is not known.
Nutrients are important for the growth of an infant, but researchers want to know what happens when there is an excess of them.

In these studies, researchers aimed to measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who experienced preterm birth, and also to determine whether preterm birth causes elevated levels of any of the micronutrients investigated.
Researchers collected blood samples from exactly 181 women shortly after they gave birth at two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital city of Malawi, between June 2016 and March 2017.
They sent blood samples by ship to a laboratory in Norway where they extracted serum, the pure form of blood, and measured the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.
About half of the 181 women in the study had preterm births, and researchers found very high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.

From there, they adjusted their models to include several other factors such as age, overall health, and pregnancy history to uncover the suspected reasons why certain foods might cause premature birth.

They concluded that high levels of selenium and copper did not play a significant role in causing preterm birth, but they stated that high levels of zinc increased the risk of preterm birth by more than 6 times.
High levels of copper have been a concern for researchers, due to the known health risks.
Having only 181 women participating in the study reduced the researchers' ability to accurately identify risks associated with high selenium levels, as the ideal number of participants is 600.
The regular foods consumed by participants have not been investigated to identify potential sources of the three nutrients, and their Body Mass Index (BMI) statistics have not been reported.
These are the first studies of their kind that measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in pregnant women in Malawi.
Africa has the highest rates of preterm births - over 18% compared to Western countries at 5%, therefore researchers want to know if nutrition plays a role in this.
Behavior of Habitat Acquisition, Returning to Original Habitats and Protecting Habitats with the Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Animals exhibit similar solitary behaviors of habitat and time which increase their survival.
Understanding behavior is a crucial step in better conservation and management, especially for endangered species.

In these studies, we conducted experiments on whether the Pancake tortoise has the ability to establish territories if it is relocated from one place to another and also investigated its return to its previous territories and the protection of its territories against different species in its natural habitats in Kitui County, Kenya.

The behavior of 39 tortoises residing within 12 isolated rock crevices was investigated from July 2020 to June 2022 using radio tracking, camera monitoring, and combining group condition sampling with ad libitum sampling.
Fourteen tortoises were fitted with radio transmitters and relocated from their rocky habitats to a distant location from their homes, and their movement and behavior were monitored.

Except for only two turtles that adapted well to the new environments they were relocated to, all other turtles attempted to find a home, with 46.15% of them retracing their paths to return to their previous habitats where they successfully returned, and 15.38% managed to reach areas believed to be close to their homes.
Successfully obtaining a home in new habitats provides evidence that there is the ability to return to original habitats for these types of organisms.

The analysis of tortoise residency in burrows showed that there is no significant statistical difference between the numbers of tortoises present initially in burrows where the average duration of those present exceeded 162 days of sampling (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P >0.05), thus continuing to support the return to initial habitats particularly for these types of organisms.

In one instance, camera trapping and ad libitum sampling demonstrated that Pancake tortoises can defend their territories where their shells provide significant protection against other incoming threats.
The lost pancake tortoises have the ability to surprise with their 'homecoming'.

Researchers made a surprising discovery when investigating the behavior of pancake tortoises from East Africa (Malacochersus tornieri): these animals are able to retrace their way back home after being displaced far away.
Understanding how and why they do this can be important for the conservation of these important species.
The behavior of finding a shelter exhibited by turtles is called "finding a home," and many other animals are also capable of doing this.
The ability to return to specific locations allows animals to return to food, mates, and their habitats, which can improve their chances of survival and reproduction.

Although the behavior of returning home has been studied in both marine and freshwater turtles, researchers in these studies state that we still know very little about the nesting of turtles (habitats suitable for turtles).
In these studies, researchers aimed to understand more about the behavior of pancake tortoises in their natural habitats among rock crevices.
They studied these animals as they moved and fed, and also when they went to rest in rock crevices or on rock ledges.
Researchers monitored groups of pancake tortoises for nearly two years, and they set up cameras to record videos of these animals when they were not being observed.
They also attached radio transmitters to 14 turtles.
These are small devices that allow researchers to track animal movements and to assess where they spend their time during the day and night.
From there, the researchers relocated some of the tracked turtles to a new location, to facilitate easier investigation.
What surprised the researchers even now is that two of the turtles began to return to their original locations, which are between 1 and 2.5 kilometers away from where they were released.
This occurred when researchers decided to remove many of the animals from their habitats, to see if they would exhibit similar behaviors of 'returning home'.

Interestingly, about half of the turtles were able to find their way back to the rocky ledges where they originally resided before being displaced, often traveling more than 1.5 kilometers to get there.
Another 15% of them were able to return to their general residential area, but they could not find the stone steps that were originally taken.
Researchers also found that different rock formations typically had an equal number of turtles resting on them, suggesting that turtles consistently use the same locations to rest.
Camera trap images also showed that male tortoises were defending their territories, causing them to fight other males when they attempted to enter their territories or on rocky outcrops.

Researchers state that this is the first time the behavior of returning to resting places has been observed in pancake tortoises, and that their findings indicate that these animals prefer to stay and rest in similar locations whenever possible.
Their research did not explain how the turtles found their way back home, therefore future researchers should focus their studies on understanding this important aspect.
Because animals sometimes need to be relocated to new conservation areas, this information will help conservation workers ensure that tortoises remain safe in their new habitats.
The research was a collaboration between scientists from Kenya and China, and it contributes to our understanding of behavior in terms of homing in turtles and other animals.
Pharmacokinetics of High-Dose Oral Plasmodium Drug Compared to Rifampicin Administered Intravenously in Patients with Meningitis Inflammation of the Brain Membrane:
Controlled non-randomized trials
Higher doses of intramuscular rifampicin can improve outcomes in reducing inflammation of the brain membrane but are not feasible in severely constrained environments.

We suggest that the use of plasma rifampicin will be similar between the oral dose of 35 mg/kg of body weight and the intramuscular dose of 20 mg/kg, which is recommended for efficacy trials to treat inflammation of the brain membrane.
We conducted non-discriminatory pharmacokinetic studies of two groups based on clinical trials of intensive antimicrobial treatment for the management of meningitis inflammation.
Participants with HIV infection and meningitis of the brain membrane were involved from South African hospitals and were randomly assigned to three different rifampicin dosage groups.
the basic dose (oral administration 10 mg/kg), the high dose (oral administration 35 mg/kg), and the intramuscular injection (20 mg/kg).
A comprehensive pharmacokinetic sampling was conducted on day 3.
Data was described using non-compartmental analysis, and applications were compared using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Forty-six participants were sampled for pharmacokinetics (baseline, n = 17; high oral dose, n = 15; intramuscular injection, n = 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm3).

The geometric mean of rifampicin between the time-concentration curve from 0 to 24 hours (AUC0–24) was 42.9mg · h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0mg · h/ml) for the baseline dose, 295.2mg · h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8mg · h/ml) for the high oral dose, and 206.5mg · h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8mg · h/ml) for the intramuscular injection.

Rifampicin AUC0–24 GMR was 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21) and the maximum concentration of the drug in serum (Cmax) GMR was 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) for the orally administered drug compared to the intramuscular injection dose.
Plasma rifampicin AUC0–24 was higher following an oral dose of 35-mg/kg compared to the standard dose of 20-mg/kg in the first few days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The findings support the orally administered dosage of rifampicin in future trials for the treatment of meningitis.
High-dose pills can be tested on HIV patients who have TB co-infection.

Researchers have confirmed that it is important to start by conducting tests to determine if high doses of the drug rifampicin can save HIV patients who have complications of brain membrane inflammation.
Up to 3 out of every 5 HIV patients who are also infected with cryptococcal meningitis die from this disease, which attacks the central nervous system.
Survivors are often left with long-term damage to their spinal cord and critical nerves originating from the brain.
This can affect their emotions and behavior.
Some patients have rashes or blisters, or their facial features or bodies are swelling.
Rifampicin, a powerful antibiotic used against tuberculosis, is often administered in pill form to try to kill the bacteria that cause inflammation of the brain lining.
Patients who are severely ill have difficulty swallowing pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered intravenously (through injections) in liquid form.
A catheter is inserted into the patient's vein so that the fluid can flow into the body.
No further tests have been conducted to reveal how a patient's body responds to the drug when this method is used.
Treatment of an intramuscular injection requires multiple supplies, hospital admission, and a trained healthcare worker who knows how to properly administer the injection.
Therefore, it is not necessarily an option in resource-limited settings of the world.
Doctors already know that rifampicin is not well accepted by the fluid of the brain, spinal cord, and liver, where bacteria can hide.
This is why high doses are necessary to effectively kill all bacteria in the patient's body.
However, the researchers were not certain about how well and safely the high dosage could work.

Researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom were therefore seeking to discover, using a small number of patients, whether it was safe to administer high doses of rifampicin in pills or by injection, and how their bodies would respond to each form.
It is important to know this before other researchers begin large trials or studies on how they plan to administer high doses of rifampicin to many patients.
One of the three types of rifampicin treatments was given to 46 South African patients with HIV infection and meningitis inflammation.
The first group was the standard treatment with pills currently given to patients, making a total of 10mg of rifampicin per kilogram of the patient's weight.
One group was given a high dosage of pills at 35 milligrams per kilogram of the patient's body weight.
The third group was given 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight by injection into the thigh.
Blood samples were taken from patients after three days.
Subsequently, the researchers analyzed how rifampicin was present in their blood plasma (the liquid component of blood).
Higher levels of rifampicin were found in the bodies of patients who were given high-dose pills compared to those who were given an injection or a standard dose.
The concentration of the drug in the blood plasma was similar to that of the high dose and the intramuscular injection.
The mixture exceeded when patients only received the baseline level.
According to researchers, this indicates that the health of patients suffering from meningitis can be improved if they receive higher doses of rifampicin.
It does not matter whether they receive it in pill form or by injection - what is important is that they receive high doses, as their bodies are able to maintain high levels of its compounds.
The results support the findings of studies conducted in the countries of Uganda and Indonesia.
Two small trials in Indonesia suggested that the lives of many patients could be saved if they were given high doses of rifampicin either orally or by injection.
Unfortunately, researchers warn that only a small number of participants were involved in the studies more than they had anticipated, which could lead to the unreliability of their results.
Research was conducted in South Africa.
They support a strategy to conduct trials to assess whether it would be beneficial to give HIV patients with symptoms of meningitis high doses of rifampicin.
It is anticipated that this type of treatment will save many lives in Africa and in other parts of the world where meningitis is a major problem.
Can the use of combined compost and biochar improve the quality of soils in heavily degraded coastal rangelands?

The SARS-CoV-2 lineage (A.23.1) with a mutated spike has emerged and is affecting the current outbreak in Uganda.
Genomic studies of SARS-CoV-2 in Uganda provide an opportunity to offer an accurate description of the virus's emergence in this small landlocked country in East Africa.

Here we show the current evolution of the epidemic in the country with the emerging new lineage A.23 evolving into A.23.1, which is currently leading in cases in Uganda and has also spread to 26 other countries.
Although the actual changes in A.23.1 as they have been altered differ from the changes in variants of concern (VOC), the mutation shows integration into a similar set of proteins.

The spike protein coding region of A.23.1 has accumulated mutations similar to many of the mutations observed in VOC, including a mutation at position 613, which is a mutation at a cleavage site that enhances a critical amino acid point, and numerous mutations in the immunogenic N-terminal domain.
Moreover, the A.23.1 lineage alters mutations in non-spike proteins that are shown by other VOCs (nsp6, ORF8, and ORF9).

The impact of the A.23.1 variant's therapeutic interventions is not yet well understood, however, it is important to continue monitoring this variant, along with a rapid assessment of the effects of spike protein mutations on the efficacy of the vaccine.
Researchers report on the mutation of the SARS-CoV-2 variant in Uganda.
In 2021, researchers reported that a new variant of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes Covid-19, emerged in Uganda and spread to 26 other countries.
They named this variant "A.23.1", indicating that most of its mutations are similar to those of proteins that researchers have identified in other variants of concern worldwide during this period.
Scientists are tracking the pattern of how coronavirus variants evolve to better understand how vaccines can work more effectively against new variants.
Covid-19 has killed many people across the world.
In a process known as genomic surveillance, scientists monitor how the virus's genetic material and proteins change as it spreads.
They use this information to control the disease and guide the development of a vaccine.
For example, by understanding the structure of viral spike proteins, researchers can design more accurate vaccines targeting these proteins to help prevent the virus from entering human cells.
In these studies, researchers focused particularly on how SARS-CoV-2 was mutating in the country of Uganda.
Researchers have demonstrated the genetic sequences of the virus on COVID-19 positive samples collected across the country of Uganda.

They used computer software to trace the lineage (or family history) of the new variant they identified in this way (called A.23.1), and they were also able to determine where the variant falls within the SARS-CoV-2 lineage.
Their results showed that the A.23.1 variant evolved from another variant called A.23, and it was detected in 90% of all samples with transmission.
In other words, it controlled samples from Uganda starting from October 2020.
They also found that the A.23.1 variant had several mutations in the spike protein similar to those observed in other variants of concern.
Mutations can increase the likelihood that a variant spreads easily (spreads rapidly), and significantly hinder vaccines and treatments.
Research contributes to current efforts to track SARS-CoV-2 variants worldwide.
The results add to the growing evidence that SARS-CoV-2 is rapidly evolving as it spreads to more people and evades vaccines.
However, more research is needed to fully understand what the roles or functions of the spike protein mutations in the A.23.1 variant might be.
Researchers suggest that more genomic studies be conducted to help us understand how virus variants evade available vaccines in Uganda and other countries.
They also state that monitoring international travel is important for researchers to better understand how the virus spreads within a country.

Research on Events Documenting the Causes and Conditions Leading to Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting in Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya
Female genital mutilation/cutting is a harmful traditional practice that violates women's rights and has very adverse health consequences.
The document outlines the reasons and circumstances that lead to the removal/cutting of female genital organs (FGM/C) in specific contexts in three countries – Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya.

Information was collected by conducting household surveys with young people (aged 15-24) and through focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, and interviews with key informants who are young people and community stakeholders in 2016 and 2017.
Descriptive statistics and content analysis of the projects were conducted.

Research findings confirm some of the reasons for FGM/C that have been documented by previous studies, which have noted that these reasons are closely related, and that gender-related customs are the main causes.
In all three cases, these reasons lead to the alteration of women's bodies to result in a 'traditional' body that is acceptable in an unchanging state preferred by men.
This concludes with a 'clean body' in Indonesia, a 'matured body' in Ethiopia, and a 'grown person's body' in Kenya.
Healthcare workers and parents play a crucial role in making decisions regarding FGM/C at all levels.
In Kenya, particularly, girls discuss the roles they play regarding decisions about FGM/C as they will be adults during the initiation ceremony.

Research reveals how changing legal and social conditions in various contexts bring about changes in the practice of FGM/C, which leads to treatment related to FGM/C in Indonesia, where the age of female genital cutting was reduced in Kenya and the clandestine practice of FGM/C in Ethiopia.
Two events highlight a significant difference in the practice of FGM/C and what they mean according to the girls and their communities.
There is a need for us to continue examining the role played by parents in decision-making.
Due to the interactions between the two drivers of FGM/C in each context, studies conclude that context-related approaches should be adopted within the frameworks of creating long-term change.
To prevent female genital mutilation, first we need to understand why this occurs.
Female genital mutilation, which is the practice where female genital organs are cut or removed, still occurs illegally or secretly in countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.
Researchers state that understanding why this occurs is crucial to preventing this harmful practice, and to preventing the health and psychological issues that women experience as a result of it.
In parts of Africa and Asia, female genital mutilation (FGM), sometimes referred to as 'female circumcision', is still commonly practiced.
Many people falsely believe that FGM is necessary for women to have proper lives or to make women respectable (lack dignity and be submissive), and to ensure that they will be able to have children.
FGM is not necessary for some of these things according to scientific evidence.
In many cases, however, children who undergo FGM end up having health problems later in their lives, such as experiencing severe infections, difficulty urinating, and mental health issues.
Because this work is very dangerous and violates women's human rights, many countries have made it illegal, yet people still do it secretly.
In these studies, researchers aimed to understand more about how FGM occurs in different countries, and what people believe about this practice.
Therefore, they collected information about FGM in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.

In each country, researchers conducted interviews with people about this practice, including parents, youth, traditional leaders, health workers, and 'cutters' (older women who performed FGM on girls).
In some cases, they asked individuals questions one-on-one, but they also held discussions with groups of people, including young people and adolescents, who had experienced FGM firsthand.
Researchers discovered that the reasons for FGM, the way it was performed, and beliefs about this practice varied from one country to another.
They also discovered that many people still do it, even in places where it was illegal to do so.

For example, in Indonesia, traditional practitioners used a knife or a similar tool to cut a part of the female genitalia (an organ often responsible for sexual pleasure in women) when a girl reached the age of 40.
People believed that this helped to 'remove impurity' and that it was important for religious reasons.
In Ethiopia, FGM occurred in the past, sometimes when infants were as young as 7 years old.
Researchers revealed that people there believed that this would ensure that a girl would become a 'better woman' one day, and that she would have respect, and that she would not defy her husband.
Many people also believed that FGM makes childbirth easier, but in fact, it can make it very difficult to deliver a baby.
Even though in Kenya, FGM indicated that a girl had reached womanhood, and that typically this occurred later in her life, when she was in her teenage years.

In some cases, however, they found that girls undergo FGM as young as 8 years old, and that many girls end up pregnant while still in their teenage years, because they were considered mature enough to engage in sexual activity after undergoing FGM.
Researchers state that their findings indicate that there are many different reasons why FGM still occurs.
As societal norms and concepts change, the way it is done and where it is done also changes.
For example, parents might attempt to do it secretly even though it is illegal, because they believe it is necessary for their daughters' physical well-being or to find a better husband.
It is important to recognize that because FGM is illegal in some places, investigating this issue can be difficult, and people may not always provide truthful answers about this issue.

In the future, in addition to making it illegal, researchers suggest that governments and health authorities should commit to preventing FGM by addressing the misconceptions people have about this practice and educating them about its dangers.

The research was a collaboration among scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands, and forms part of a larger project called the 'Yes I Do' program, which aims to reduce adolescent pregnancies, child marriages, and FGM.

Traditional Use of Home Garden Plants by the Indigenous Community in Northwestern Ethiopia
Information about plants in home gardens in Northwestern Ethiopia in general, and particularly in the Gozamin district, has not been given sufficient research attention.
The purpose of these studies is to better understand information about plants and the importance of home gardens to the culture.
A stratified sampling method was used to divide participants into groups based on agricultural and ecological differences in selected districts.

Data from home gardens was collected by dividing the home gardens into four quadrants, the first quadrant extending from the farmer's house up to 10m, the second quadrant from 10m to 20m, the third quadrant from 20m to 30m, and the fourth quadrant from 30m to 40m horizontally using the farmer's house as a reference point considering the size of the garden.
Briefly arranged interviews were conducted to document the expert knowledge about plant species.
A total of 238 culturally significant plant species from 81 families were identified.
Above 39% were shrubs, 29% were trees, and 6% were vines.
Perennial plants constituted the majority of the cultivated species (83%), while annual plants made up (17%).
The Poaceae family had the highest number of species, with 22, followed by Fabaceae, which had 21, and Asteraceae, which had 15.

Of the reported plants, 140 (58.6%) were species used for environmental purposes, 84 (35%) for edible vegetables, 83 (34.7%) for medicinal plant species, 39 (16.3%) for fodder species, 57 (23.8%) for plants producing materials, 60 (25%) for firewood species, 50 (21%) for domestic use plants, and 1 (0.4%) for ornamental purposes.

The selection of the matrix directly revealed that Cordia Africana is an important plant in significant traditional practices in the region, which was also at high risk of extinction, followed by Ficus sur.
The primary benefit of using Cordia Africana in construction and its secondary value was in the production of medicinal plants.
The Sorensen similarity index for 64% of the sites surveyed was below 0.5.
The results showed that home gardens are used for various reasons, with production programs for a long period.
Food security and biodiversity conservation continue to be supported by the traditional knowledge of communities governed by chiefs, which aligns with their home gardens.

The slight similarity of plant species in the environment between the districts indicated that there was a high diversity of plants, which was caused by the different types of agricultural practices and ecology between the districts.
Ethiopian landscapes support food production and conservation.

Researchers state that the majority of residents in Ethiopia cultivate food plants, ornamental plants, medicinal plants, and plants for feeding animals, providing shade, or building fences for their gardens.
They analyzed the gardens to see how important they are in ensuring food production and helping to conserve the environment.
People around the world create gardens to produce food, make money, and for other cultural purposes.
Reserves protect important plants that are often rare or disappearing in other environments.
In Ethiopia, not much research has been conducted on what residents are actually planting in their gardens.
In these studies, researchers aimed to investigate the plants that residents of the Gozamin district, Northwest Ethiopia, cultivated in their gardens and what they used them for.
They selected and counted plants in 357 plots in the area.
They conducted interviews with residents regarding the reasons they use plants.
Researchers also found that all the gardens in Gozamin were surpassed by one hectare in size.
They collected and identified 238 different plant species.
The majority (83%) of the plants were cultivated year-round, with only (17%) being cultivated seasonally.
Their results showed that the residents used plants to produce food, medicine, fodder (animal feed), and for other cultural reasons.
Most plants had more than one benefit.
For example, the large-leaved tree in the Northern region could be used for medicine, decoration, fodder, shade, building a fence, and other traditional purposes.
More than half (59%) of the plants were used for environmental purposes such as building fences, providing shade, and decoration.
Researchers stated that this helped protect the environment.
Plants used to build a fence also helped protect farm products.
A slightly higher proportion (35%) of the plants were cultivated for food production, such as fruits, vegetables, cereals, and spices.
However, they stated that the gardens in the area were producing a lot of fruits.
Researchers stated that 35% of plants were used as traditional medicine to help treat humans and animals, while 21% were used for cultural and religious purposes, smoking, incense, and packaging.
Some plants (17%) were used as fodder to feed cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
Some (24%) were used as construction materials, to make decorations in gardens, for thatching with grass, and for weaving ropes.
As most rural residents reported using wood, 25% of the plants were used for that purpose.
Researchers stated that only one plant (0.4%) has been shown to be used for medicinal purposes.

They also stated that the way plants were distributed in the environment was influenced by the environment, what people preferred to eat, as well as the financial situation of households and business demands.
For example, the area called Wenka, which had irrigation water and was close to the capital city, had many gardens and reported 130 different plant species.

Researchers stated that their results confirmed that indeed farmers were planting a high number of different types of crops in their fields, and using them for various purposes.
